title: Trump Forces G7 Into a 100-Million-Barrel Emergency Oil Release as Yemen's Government Opens a New Front Against the Houthis and Ethiopia Retakes Mekelle
subhead: The US strong-armed its allies into tapping strategic reserves to cool fuel prices, while the Iran-US war widened into Yemen and a four-year-old Tigray peace deal collapsed on the battlefield.

sections.heading: G7 Taps Emergency Reserves After Trump Threatens a Diesel Export Ban
sections.body:
The G7 agreed to release up to 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over the next four months, including a front-loaded diesel release over the next 20 days, according to the Sydney Morning Herald. The decision came in response to a Trump threat to ban US diesel exports — a direct hit at the EU and UK, which are heavily reliant on US imports with the northern winter approaching. Trump has since said 'we were never going to do it', framing the threat as leverage rather than policy.

The market reaction was muted. Brent dipped below $100 a barrel on the announcement before bouncing back above $102, and US gasoline prices remain about 40 percent higher than a year ago, with diesel more than 70 percent higher, per the same report. Reuters reported Asian stocks upbeat and the dollar wobbling as Fed hike bets recede, rather than a decisive oil reprieve.
sections.whyItMatters: The episode shows Washington treating allied energy security as a bargaining chip. Even a 100-million-barrel release is described as a palliative for market damage caused by the Middle East war — it buys time before the US midterms, it does not fix the underlying supply problem.

sections.heading: Yemen's Government Declares a Full Offensive as the War Widens
sections.body:
Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi announced a nationwide military campaign to restore state authority and retake Houthi-held territory, according to the BBC and Asharq Al-Awsat. Ynet reported the Saudi-backed government is assembling a campaign involving roughly 100,000 troops aimed at strategic territory and the Bab el-Mandab Strait. The Houthis, meanwhile, are advancing on Taiz and, per Newswav, have launched missiles and drones toward Saudi oil infrastructure, threatening regional supplies.

The move opens a new ground front in the wider Iran-US war. SBS reported that the Houthis have controlled most of Yemen's populated areas since the conflict began, and that the government is vowing to reclaim it while the rebels make fresh battlefield gains.
sections.whyItMatters: Bab el-Mandab is one of the world's two critical Gulf chokepoints. A full Yemeni ground war — with the Houthis striking Saudi oil — turns a proxy conflict into an active threat to Red Sea and Gulf shipping at the same moment Hormuz remains contested.

sections.heading: Ethiopian Forces Retake Mekelle, and the Tigray Peace Deal Unravels
sections.body:
Ethiopian federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force fighters took control of Mekelle, the Tigray regional capital, after the TPLF said it had withdrawn and would operate its administration from elsewhere, Al Jazeera and Reuters reported. Government forces and allied militiamen entered the city on Saturday, with a pro-government source, a humanitarian worker and a resident confirming control to Reuters.

The capture comes less than four years after the November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended the 2020-22 war, which killed hundreds of thousands. In July the TPLF declared the Pretoria deal effectively collapsed, accusing Addis Ababa of failing to implement it; the government denied that and blamed the TPLF. Disputed territories, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces were never resolved. Residents in Addis Ababa have also reported hearing explosions in the capital, and Ethiopia accuses Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing the rebels — all three deny it.
sections.whyItMatters: A return to full-scale war in Tigray would destabilize the Horn of Africa and reopen a conflict that already displaced millions. It also drags in Ethiopia's regional rivals, turning an internal dispute into a wider contest involving Egypt and Eritrea.

sections.heading: Japan Builds a Dedicated Intelligence Agency as China Tensions Mount
sections.body:
Japan is standing up its own spy agency 'with the utmost urgency' amid escalating tensions with China, ABC News reported, while CNBC reported that Japanese companies are retreating from China at a record pace. Taiwan's envoy is pressing the Trump administration over a stalled arms sale, per the Japan Times. Meanwhile, Taiwan's defense ministry logged continued PLA activity in the waters and airspace around the island on October 5.

Reuters reported that, per US sources, Washington does not expect a Chinese invasion of Taiwan next year despite the 2027 planning timeline — a signal that US assessments see near-term risk as lower than the rhetoric suggests.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan creating a standalone intelligence service is a structural shift in how a pacifist constitution-bound ally organizes for conflict. Paired with record corporate withdrawals from China, it marks a deepening decoupling between East Asia's two largest economies.

sections.heading: Rubio Tours NATO Allies as Russia's Threat and the Middle East War Set the Agenda
sections.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio travels to Iceland, Greece and Portugal from October 5-8 for talks on security, defense, energy, economic cooperation and technology, RFE/RL reported. He begins in Reykjavik on Arctic security, then Athens for the sixth US-Greece Strategic Dialogue — with Ukraine and the Middle East on the agenda — and Lisbon for defense and tech talks. The trip spans Iceland's North Atlantic role, Greece's Eastern Mediterranean position and Portugal's importance to US Atlantic operations.

In parallel, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russian intelligence could target Ukraine's NATO supporters with hybrid strikes, and a Russian drone struck close to the Polish-Ukrainian border, heightening concerns along NATO's eastern flank, per Brussels Post. The EU also approved five shared defense programs including drone swarms and counter-drone systems, and six nations — France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Sweden and the UK — moved a long-range strike missile initiative into implementation.
sections.whyItMatters: The Atlantic alliance is simultaneously managing Russian hybrid pressure in Europe and an active Middle East war. European moves on joint drones and long-range missiles show allies hedging against US distraction — building capability they may not be able to assume Washington will supply.

bottomLine: Today's through-line is allies being stretched by US-led wars they did not choose. Trump forced the G7 to drain strategic reserves to contain fuel prices he partly caused; Yemen's government opened a new front against the Houthis while the rebels hit Saudi oil; and Ethiopia's four-year-old Tigray peace deal collapsed with the retaking of Mekelle. Each is a different theater, but the pattern is the same — the post-2022 order is fraying, and the states absorbing the shock are often not the ones setting the agenda.
